target.title: Speech Synthesis from Text and Ultrasound Tongue Image-based Articulatory Input
target.venue: arXiv preprint (eess.AS); no workshop or journal venue is stated on the first page

read.pdf: Fig. 1–2; Tables 1–5; all six pages visually checked

entries.text: The paper claims novelty in using ultrasound-derived articulatory features as additional input to HMM- or DNN-TTS; it says medical-imaging-derived articulatory features had not been used this way before.
entries.condition: Prior-art claim about UTI/MRI-derived features used as additional TTS input.

entries.text: The proposed system extends vocoder-based DNN-TTS with PCA-compressed ultrasound input and compares text-only, ultrasound-only, and combined input conditions.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent acoustic-feature prediction; output is synthesized with WORLD.
entries.quote: We compare text-only, ultrasound-only, and combined inputs.

entries.text: The corpus subset contains eight English subjects: four male (03mn, 04me, 05ms, 07me) and four female (01fi, 02fe, 06fe, 09fe).
entries.condition: UltraSuite-TaL80; each subject has parallel speech and ultrasound recordings.

entries.text: Audio is digitized at 48 kHz; midsagittal ultrasound was recorded with an Articulate Instruments Micro system at 81.5 fps, synchronized with the audio; lip video was unused.
entries.condition: UltraSuite-TaL80 acquisition; midsagittal UTI; lip video recorded but excluded.
entries.quote:
In
parallel with speech (digitized at 48 kHz), the tongue movement
was recorded in midsagittal orientation using the “Micro” ultra-
sound system of Articulate Instruments Ltd. at 81.5 fps.

entries.text: Each speaker contributed roughly 200 sentences and about 15 minutes of recordings; the authors split the utterances 85/10/5 into train/validation/test.
entries.unit: sentences per speaker; minutes per speaker; percent train/validation/test
entries.condition: Per-speaker UltraSuite-TaL80 recordings; utterance-level partitioning is described, but exact counts are not given.
entries.quote: which we partitioned into training, validation and test sets in a 85-10-5 ratio

entries.text: The ultrasound frames were resized from 64×842 to 64×128 pixels using bicubic interpolation.
entries.condition: Raw ultrasound image preprocessing before PCA.

entries.text: The authors target 70% retained image variance and use 128 PCA coefficients.
entries.condition: PCA representation of resized ultrasound frames.
entries.quote: While calculating the PCA, we aimed at keeping the 70% of the variance of the original images, thus having 128 coefﬁcients.

entries.text: Ultrasound is resampled to 200 Hz to match acoustic features at a 5 ms frame shift.
entries.condition: UTI and acoustic-feature frame synchronization.
entries.quote:
To be in synchrony with the acoustic
features (frame shift of 5 ms), the ultrasound data was resam-
pled to 200 Hz.

entries.text: The DNN predicts WORLD acoustic/excitation features at 5 ms frames: 60-dimensional MGC, 5-dimensional BAP, and 1-dimensional LF0, with delta and delta-delta features.
entries.unit: ms frame step; MGC dimensions; BAP dimensions; LF0 dimension
entries.condition: WORLD vocoder; acoustic feature regression from text-derived linguistic features and, for multimodal systems, PCA-compressed UTI.

entries.text: The network is a feed-forward MLP with six hidden layers of 1024 neurons each and a tanh activation.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent Merlin DNN-TTS acoustic model.
entries.quote:
The DNN used here is a feed-forward multi-
layer perceptron architecture (six hidden layers, 1024 neurons
in each).

entries.text: Training uses SGD and a batch size of 256.
entries.condition: Feed-forward DNN training; optimizer is SGD.

entries.text: The stated schedule is 25 epochs, 10 warm-up epochs, early stopping, and learning rate 0.002 after warm-up with exponential decay.
entries.condition: The paper does not state the early-stopping metric or patience; repository details are recorded separately.

entries.text: Paper-stated normalization is min-max for input features and mean-variance for output acoustic features.
entries.condition: Normalization-statistic fitting scope and min-max target interval are not stated in the paper.

entries.text: Only acoustic models are trained; durations are not modeled, so no duration-based time warping is used for feature-error calculation.
entries.condition: Direct acoustic feature prediction and WORLD synthesis; no duration model.
entries.quote: We only trained an acoustic model, and the durations were not modeled.

entries.text: The baselines are text-only and ultrasound-only; text-only uses the standard Merlin recipe, while ultrasound-only replaces the linguistic-feature decision tree with an empty tree. Other training parameters are held fixed across all three input conditions.
entries.condition: Text-only, UTI-only, and text+UTI systems; acoustic model and training parameters otherwise matched.

entries.text: The paper reports validation and test MCD, BAP, F0-RMSE, F0-correlation, and F0-VUV errors; acoustic features are compared without temporal warping.
entries.condition: Per-speaker held-out development/test partitions; exact metric formulas and several units are not specified in the paper.
entries.quote: To measure the validation and test error, we calculated both spectral prediction error (Mel-Cepstral Distortion, MCD), and excitation related errors (BAP, F0-RMSE, F0-correlation, and F0-VUV).

entries.text: The paper summarizes ultrasound-only MCD as 6.9–8.4 dB across speakers.
entries.condition: Authors' rounded summary for all eight speakers and the dev/test results; see Table 1 rows for exact values.

entries.text: The paper summarizes text-only MCD as typically 5.7–6.4 dB.
entries.condition: Authors' rounded characterization of limited-data DNN-TTS; see Table 1 rows for exact dev/test values.
entries.quote: The ’txt2wav’ (text-to-speech synthesis) system can achieve signiﬁcantly lower MCD errors, which are typically in the range of DNN-TTS with limited data (5.7–6.4 dB).

entries.text: The combined system is reported as lowest in MCD, in the 5.5–6.2 dB range; the authors infer improved spectral prediction from the ultrasound input.
entries.condition: Authors' rounded summary for text+UTI across the eight speakers; see Table 1 rows for exact dev/test values.

entries.text: Authors report BAP error ordering as ultrasound-only worst, text-only next, and combined text+UTI best.
entries.condition: Per-speaker dev/test results; the paper provides no BAP unit in the table or prose.

entries.text: The authors say the additional articulatory input did not help text-to-F0 prediction by F0-RMSE, although the three systems' errors were in a similar range.
entries.condition: Per-speaker dev/test results in Table 3; full values are recorded row by row.

entries.text: Authors say F0-CORR generally benefits from added articulatory information; ultrasound-only exceeds text-only correlation for speakers 04me and 09fe.
entries.condition: Per-speaker dev/test results in Table 4; “higher” correlation is better.

entries.text: Authors report very poor voicing estimation from ultrasound-only input and no benefit from adding articulatory input to text for the voiced/unvoiced decision.
entries.condition: Per-speaker dev/test F0-VUV results in Table 5.
entries.quote: adding the articulatory information to the text input did not help to improve the voiced/unvoiced decision

entries.text: Overall, the authors claim UTI helps spectral and BAP prediction and some F0 measures, while results show strong speaker dependency.
entries.condition: Eight speaker-specific systems; objective acoustic/excitation prediction errors.
entries.quote:
Overall, we found that adding ultrasound-related articula-
tory information besides the textual input was useful for the
spectral and BAP prediction, and in some of the F0 measures.

entries.text: The authors claim ultrasound transducer-position misalignment can harm final synthesis performance.
entries.condition: The evidence is a visual association between UTI-image MSE patterns and MCD differences; exact relation remains unquantified.

entries.text: For each speaker/session, the paper compares average ultrasound images across consecutive utterances in an n×n MSE matrix, using grayscale pixels in [0,255].
entries.condition: MSE between per-utterance time-averaged UTI images; lower MSE is interpreted as greater similarity.

entries.text: The authors associate visible train-to-development/test ultrasound-image differences for 01fi, 04me, 05ms, and 07me with higher MCD, while 06fe has a homogeneous MSE matrix and lowest MCD.
entries.condition: Visual comparison of Fig. 2 with Table 1; the authors do not quantify a causal effect.
entries.quote:
For speakers 01ﬁ, 04me, 05ms, and 07me this tendency is vis-
ible, and comparing the MSE ﬁgures (Fig. 2) with the MCD
results on the development/test set (Table 1), we can observe
higher errors for them than for the remaining speakers.

entries.text: The authors concede that the exact relationship between transducer misalignment and acoustic/excitation errors remains future work.
entries.condition: Misalignment analysis is descriptive and does not establish a quantified predictive or causal relationship.
entries.quote: Quantifying the exact relation between the ultrasound transducer misalignment and the acoustic / excitation errors remains future work.

entries.text: Sec. 5: the system is not suitable for direct TTS or for a Silent Speech Interface, because the combined mapping requires both text and articulatory input; the authors call the methods a kind of scientific exploration.
entries.condition: The combined inference condition requires both modalities.
entries.quote: both text and articulatory input are required, our methods are a kind of

entries.text: Creating an average voice and adapting it to a specific speaker are left as future work.
entries.condition: The reported experiments use speaker-dependent DNNs.

entries.text: Speaker-independent training remains a challenge because the PCA representation trained on one speaker's articulatory data is not transferable to other speakers.
entries.condition: PCA representation is speaker-specific; no speaker-independent experiment is reported.

entries.text: Extension to other biosignals, including MRI or lip video, is future work.
entries.condition: Only ultrasound tongue images are evaluated in this paper; recorded lip video is unused.

entries.text: No subjective listening test or human naturalness rating is reported; the naturalness claim is supported by objective acoustic/excitation error measures only.
entries.condition: Evaluation described in the paper consists of MCD, BAP, F0-RMSE, F0-correlation, and F0-VUV; no listener protocol or rating scale is stated.
entries.quote: To measure the validation and test error, we calculated both spectral prediction error (Mel-Cepstral Distortion, MCD), and excitation related errors (BAP, F0-RMSE, F0-correlation, and F0-VUV).

entries.text: The paper does not report the random seed or number of independent training repetitions; a current repository seed is documented separately and does not establish which seed was used for the reported runs.
entries.condition: Reproducibility condition for all reported per-speaker metrics.
entries.quote: We trained the networks for 25 epochs with a warm-up of 10 epochs, applying early stopping, and a learning rate of 0.002 after that with exponential decay.

entries.text: No chance-level or trivial baseline is defined for the reported continuous acoustic/excitation error measures.
entries.condition: Comparisons are among text-only, UTI-only, and text+UTI systems; no chance benchmark is stated.

entries.text: The paper does not give exact utterance counts or identifiers per split, the number of sessions per speaker, or whether partitions are session-disjoint.
entries.condition: Per-speaker 85/10/5 ratio is stated; code gives the repository split procedure but not the corpus session protocol.

entries.text: No external language model, search decoder, or additional use-time aid is described; the reported setup predicts acoustic features from supplied text/UTI and vocodes them.
entries.condition: TTS feature prediction; not a token-recognition or beam-search task.

entries.text: Evaluation is speaker-dependent: each subject's utterances are split into train, validation, and test, so test speakers are represented in training; no held-out-speaker test is reported.
entries.condition: Within-speaker generalization to held-out utterances; speaker-independent training is explicitly future work.

entries.text: The public recipe sorts speaker filenames and assigns the first int(0.85N) utterances to train, the next int(0.10N) to validation, and the remainder to test; the split is not randomized.
entries.condition: Per-speaker filename-sorted contiguous split; the article states the ratios but omits this deterministic ordering and rounding procedure.

entries.text: The recipe fits the 128-component PCA using only frames from the training utterances, then transforms train, validation, and test images with that fitted PCA.
entries.condition: The paper reports PCA compression but omits the fitting-data scope.

entries.text: Resized grayscale UTI pixels are divided by 255 before PCA fitting and transformation.
entries.condition: Per-frame image preprocessing; this pixel scaling is not stated in the paper.

entries.text: Audio is resampled to 48 kHz, normalized by SoX to −3 dB, and cut starting 240 samples before the first ultrasound-frame timestamp.
entries.condition: Audio preprocessing; the article states 48 kHz and synchronization but not volume normalization or this trimming procedure.

entries.text: The code upsamples PCA streams by resizing the time axis with ratio 589/240 (about 81.5-to-200 Hz) and a companion script truncates each stream to the LF0 frame count.
entries.condition: UTI-to-acoustic frame alignment implementation; the paper states the target 200 Hz but not this interpolation/truncation method.

entries.text: The Merlin entry point initializes its NumPy model RNG with seed 123; its training data provider shuffles file lists with seed 271638.
entries.condition: Current linked repository implementation; paper reports no seed or repeated-run count, and source code alone does not establish the exact experimental run configuration.

entries.text: Merlin fits input min/max and output acoustic mean/std statistics on training files only and applies them to all partitions; input min-max values are mapped to 0.01–0.99.
entries.condition: Normalization statistic fitting scope and target range are not specified in the article.

entries.text: Training receives a validation set; Merlin monitors mean validation loss, saves the best-validation model, and applies early stopping after epoch 15 when the no-improvement counter exceeds its configured patience (default 5).
entries.condition: The paper says early stopping but omits the monitored criterion, checkpoint selection rule, and patience.

entries.text: The evaluation logger reports MCD and BAP in dB, F0-RMSE in Hz, F0 correlation as a coefficient, and VUV error in percent.
entries.condition: These units are absent from the paper's result-table headings; MCD's dB range is mentioned in prose.

entries.text: MCD excludes MGC coefficient 0, averages framewise spectral Euclidean distances, then applies (10/ln(10))×sqrt(2) for dB conversion.
entries.condition: Formula and coefficient handling are not stated in the article.

entries.text: BAP error is computed from framewise Euclidean differences, averaged over frames, and divided by 10 before reporting in dB.
entries.condition: The article gives BAP values and an error description but no unit or calculation details.

entries.text: F0-RMSE and F0-CORR use only frames voiced in both reference and prediction; LF0 is exponentiated to Hz, and correlation is Pearson correlation. VUV error counts voiced/unvoiced mismatches over all frames.
entries.condition: Voicing matching, conversion from log-F0, and VUV denominator are not specified in the paper.

entries.text: The acoustic output stream includes MGC, LF0, VUV, and BAP; the generated WORLD waveform uses MGC, LF0, and BAP.
entries.unit: predicted feature streams; waveform synthesis streams
entries.condition: The article lists MGC, BAP, and LF0 dimensions but does not explicitly enumerate VUV among the model outputs despite reporting F0-VUV errors.

entries.text: The authors claim combined text and articulatory input may increase synthesized-speech naturalness in limited-data scenarios compared with text-only input.
entries.condition: Claim based on eight-speaker UltraSuite-TaL experiments with roughly 200 sentences per speaker; the paper reports no subjective naturalness ratings.
entries.quote: it may increase the naturalness of synthesized speech compared to single text input.

entries.text: No statistical test, confidence interval, or uncertainty estimate is reported alongside the prose claim of significantly lower MCD.
entries.condition: Per-speaker MCD comparisons in Table 1; significance-testing method and repetitions are not stated.

entries.text: The text front-end's lexicon/vocabulary size, out-of-vocabulary handling, and grapheme-to-phoneme configuration are not described.
entries.condition: Text input is converted to linguistic features via a decision tree; no vocabulary coverage condition is reported.

entries.text: Tongue motion was imaged midsagittally using an Articulate Instruments Micro system and a 2–4 MHz, 64-element, 20-mm-radius convex transducer; the transducer was fixed with a stabilization headset.
entries.condition: Single-speaker recording setup.

entries.text: The native ultrasound acquisition rate was 82 frames per second.
entries.condition: Recording setup.

entries.text: The dataset contains 438 read-aloud sentences from one 42-year-old Hungarian female speaker.
entries.condition: One speaker; Hungarian; 438 read sentences.

entries.text: The 438 recordings were partitioned into 310 training, 41 development, and 87 test utterances.
entries.condition: Single-speaker Hungarian read-speech dataset.

entries.text: An autoencoder compresses ultrasound frames; a second DNN uses its bottleneck activations to estimate the MGC-LSP spectral vector and gain for direct speech synthesis.
entries.condition: Single-speaker Hungarian read-speech data; direct articulatory-to-acoustic mapping.

entries.text: Synthesis reused the original recorded F0; the DNN estimated the remaining MGC-LSP parameters, which were vocoded to reconstruct speech.
entries.condition: Original F0 from the corresponding speech recording was supplied at synthesis.

entries.text: Training data comprised approximately 500 paired ultrasound-video/voice commands per collaborator; both networks were speaker-dependent.
entries.condition: Two male collaborators, ages 28 and 24; speaker-dependent training; vocabulary described as various speech commands; decoding/LM and seeds not stated.

entries.text: Unchanged smart-speaker recognition success was 42.5% for Network 1, 65.0% for Network 1 + Network 2, and 90.0% for ground-truth audio; combined-model scores were 65% for each user.
entries.condition: Users A and B; four typical Alexa commands, five repetitions each (20 utterances); unchanged Amazon Echo/Echo Show; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: Google Cloud Speech-to-Text WER was 41.03% for Network 1, 33.56% for Network 2, and 20.61% for ground truth.
entries.condition: 40 speech commands from two users; Google cloud speech-to-text; same environment as smart-speaker recognition; Network 2 refers to the reported Network 2 condition; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: The smart-speaker recognition test used four typical Alexa commands, each repeated five times, for 20 utterances total.
entries.condition: Participants; typical Amazon Alexa command vocabulary; tested through unchanged Amazon Echo/Echo Show; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: The authors qualitatively judged Network 2 audio better than Network 1, while noting that the output difference was unclear; no listener-panel or MOS score is reported.
entries.condition: Training-output comparison; no formal human-listener protocol stated.

entries.text: The end-to-end silent-voicing test instructed participants not to vibrate their vocal cords, but small leaked sounds occurred; the reported 37.14 dB(A) is participant sound level, not generated-speech quality.
entries.unit: dB(A), mean peak participant sound level
entries.condition: 20 typical Alexa-command measurements; noise meter 30 cm away; background 31.0 dB(A); instructed to mouth commands as silently as possible.

entries.text: Speaker-specific CNNs used two 3×3 convolutional layers (16 then 8 filters), each with max-pooling, followed by two 1,000-unit dense layers; ReLU was used throughout.
entries.condition: Four speaker-specific models.

entries.text: Temporal context was limited to a single 64×128 ultrasound frame per input; no consecutive-frame window or recurrent architecture was used, favoring real-time suitability.
entries.condition: Single-frame UTI input.

entries.text: Three output CNNs predicted log(ContF0), log(MVF), and MGC-LSP spectral features; the spectral representation was 24-order MGC-LSP.
entries.condition: Each parameter network received 64×128 UTI images.

entries.text: The proposed continuous residual-based vocoder used ContF0 and MVF to shape voiced/residual and noise excitation, then synthesized through an MGLSA filter with the MGC stream.
entries.condition: Continuous-F0 vocoder; compared with a baseline using discontinuous F0.

entries.text: The corpus comprised four Hungarian speakers (two male, two female), each reading 209 sentences; midsagittal UTI was recorded at 81.67 fps and resized to 64×128 pixels.
entries.condition: Normal speaking ability; read-sentence recordings; vocabulary details not stated.

entries.text: Data were partitioned 85/10/5 into training, validation, and test sets; objective evaluation used nine held-out sentences per speaker.
entries.condition: Four speakers; direct UTI-to-acoustic mapping, with no vocabulary, decoding/LM, or seed details reported.

entries.text: Test-set averages: V/UV accuracy 78.84%; baseline F0 RMSE 65.34 Hz; proposed ContF0 RMSE 30.56 Hz; MVF RMSE 864.69 Hz.
entries.condition: Table 1 averages across four speakers; objective test set, nine sentences per speaker.

entries.text: MUSHRA found only a slight, nonsignificant naturalness preference for predicted ContF0/MVF paired with original spectral features; systems with all parameters predicted were rated roughly equally.
entries.condition: Online MUSHRA; three test sentences per speaker; 23 native Hungarian listeners; naturalness scale 0–100.

entries.text: For each speaker and session, the authors average each utterance's ultrasound images over time, including silence, then compare consecutive utterance means using MSE, SSIM, and CW-SSIM to form a session comparison matrix.
entries.condition: MSE is the error metric; SSIM and CW-SSIM are similarity metrics.
entries.quote:
For a session,
all of the consecutive utterances are compared with each other.

entries.text: The Hungarian children dataset contains two child speakers (a girl and a boy), recorded in five sessions over two years; the nonsense-word material uses Hungarian vowels.
entries.condition: Hungarian children dataset

entries.text: UltraSuite provides Scottish English child ultrasound data from typically developed and speech-sound-disordered groups; the study used only the typically developed UXTD subset. The paper does not give an overall speaker or session count for this subset.
entries.condition: UltraSuite; UXTD subset only

entries.text: Large MSE and low SSIM/CW-SSIM indicate recording corruption or problems that may arise from transducer misalignment or insufficient gel; the paper reports no direct recognition or synthesis outcome.
entries.condition: Across ultrasound utterance recordings
entries.quote:
The results suggest that large val-
ues of Mean Square Error (MSE) and small values of Structural
Similarity Index (SSIM) and Complex Wavelet SSIM indicate
corruptions or issues during the data recordings, which can ei-
ther be caused by transducer misalignment or lack of gel.

entries.text: Title: Quantification of Transducer Misalignment in Ultrasound Tongue Imaging. Authors: Tamás Gábor Csapó and Kele Xu. First-public month: August 2020.
entries.condition: arXiv v1 dated 6 Aug 2020

entries.text: The paper credits Cao et al. with integrating EMA-based articulatory data into DNN-TTS, either as joint training targets or through an additional articulatory-to-acoustic DNN; naturalness and speaker identity improved over a baseline without articulatory data.
entries.condition: Related work as described by the target (Sec. 1.3); Cao et al. is not in the wiki.

entries.text: Ling et al. integrated EMA-based features into HMM-TTS by estimating the joint distribution of acoustic and articulatory features during training.
entries.condition: Related work as described by the target (Sec. 1.3).

entries.text: Synthesized samples are published on a web page; no listener rated them in the paper.
entries.condition: Sec. 3
entries.quote: Several synthesized samples can be found at

entries.text: Sec. 5: all previous articulatory-TTS works used EMA; they included articulatory information as input [18, Cao et al.], as the target, or as an internal representation.
entries.condition: Authors' own related-work summary.
entries.quote: it might be the input [18], or the target of the machine learning method [14, 15, 16], or also an internal representation [18]

entries.text: Sec. 5: previous works applied EMA, a point-tracking device, whose data processing differs significantly from ultrasound.
entries.quote: All of these previous works are applying EMA as articulatory data, which is a point tracking equipment

entries.text: Midsagittal ultrasound recorded with the Micro system at 81.67 fps.
entries.condition: Four Hungarian speakers.
entries.quote: The tongue movement was recorded in midsagittal orientation using the “Micro” ultra- sound system of Articulate Instruments Ltd. at 81.67 fps.

entries.text: MUSHRA listening test: each sentence rated by 23 native Hungarian speakers.
entries.condition: Ultrasound-to-speech, Hungarian.
entries.quote: Each sentence was rated by 23 native Hungarian speakers

entries.text: 3D CNN reduced test MSE by about 21% relative to the 2D CNN.
entries.condition: Ultrasound-to-speech feature regression; baseline 2D CNN.
entries.quote: The 2D CNN network was superior to the fully connected network, but the 3D CNN clearly outperformed it, reducing the MSE on the test set by about 21% in a relative sense.

entries.text: Sec. 5 opens the concession: the proposed system is not suitable for direct TTS or for a Silent Speech Interface.
entries.quote: system proposed in the current study is not suitable for direct

questions.q: Did combined text+UTI input improve held-out test MCD over text-only input?
questions.answer: Yes. Table 1 gives lower combined-system test MCD for every evaluated speaker; the per-speaker values are recorded in t35–t42.

questions.q: Does the paper directly demonstrate greater perceived naturalness?
questions.answer: No subjective ratings or listening protocol are reported. The authors make a naturalness claim and support it with objective feature-error measures; see t16, t19, t33, and t92.

questions.q: Can the combined system be used as a text-free Silent Speech Interface, and how broad is its speaker generalization?
questions.answer: The authors say both text and articulatory input are required; experiments are speaker-dependent, with average-voice/adaptation and speaker-independent training left as future work.

questions.q: What important reproducibility and evaluation details are absent from the paper but available in the linked implementation?
questions.answer: The repository specifies deterministic filename-ordered splits, training-only PCA and normalization statistics, seeds, validation-loss checkpoint selection, metric units/formulas, and audio/UTI preprocessing details.

questions.q: What does the cited prior arxiv-2008.02470 measure for transducer misalignment, on which data, and does it link misalignment to synthesis output?
questions.answer: Per-utterance time-averaged ultrasound images compared across consecutive utterances with MSE, SSIM and CW-SSIM; Hungarian children (2 speakers, 5 sessions) and UltraSuite UXTD; large MSE / low SSIM flag recording corruption from misalignment or lack of gel; no recognition or synthesis outcome.
